title: STM study of single phosphorus incorporation into silicon by heating PBr3 on Si(100)
authors: Tatiana V. Pavlova, Vladimir M. Shevlyuga
abstract: The objective of miniaturizing doped areas in silicon, with the ultimate goal of achieving atomic-precision doping, requires a fundamental understanding of the dopant incorporation process at the atomic level. We present a combined scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and density functional theory (DFT) investigation of single phosphorus atom incorporation into the Si(100) surface. Phosphorus was supplied via PBr3 molecules, which completely dissociate on Si(100) at room temperature. By performing in situ annealing within the STM, we directly tracked the same phosphorus atom before and after heating. Upon annealing, the P atom undergoes an exchange with a nearby Si atom, forming a stable P-Si-Br complex with a Br atom located atop the Si atom of the heterodimer. The activation barrier calculated using DFT is consistent with our observation of doping starting at temperatures as low as 175 C. These results provide detailed atomic-scale insight into the phosphorus incorporation pathway and offer a foundation for improving methods of precise, single-atom doping in silicon.
summary: This work provides an atomic-scale investigation into how phosphorus dopants incorporate into silicon surfaces using PBr3 precursors. By combining STM imaging with DFT calculations, the researchers mapped the incorporation pathway, demonstrating that the process forms a stable P-Si-Br heterodimer structure at low temperatures. This offers crucial foundational knowledge for achieving highly precise doping necessary for advanced semiconductor devices.
main_problem: The study aims to understand the fundamental, atomic-scale mechanism by which single phosphorus dopant atoms are incorporated into the Si(100) surface.
main_result: Phosphorus incorporation occurs via an exchange reaction forming a stable P-Si-Br heterodimer structure, with DFT calculations confirming a low activation barrier of 1.44 eV consistent with experimental observations starting at 175°C.
method: The research combines in situ Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) experiments to track atoms and Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations using the Nudged Elastic Band method to map energy barriers.
model_or_system: The physical system is the Si(100) surface, studied using PBr3 as a precursor. The investigation tracks single P atoms undergoing exchange reactions with Si atoms upon controlled heating within the STM chamber.
key_observables: STM images showing surface features like depressions (embedded P) and protrusions (adsorbed Br), and calculated energy barrier profiles for atomic movement.
important_parameters: Low temperature doping initiation at 175°C; activation barriers calculated via DFT (e.g., 1.44 eV for P incorporation).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that tracking individual atoms in situ provides a direct pathway, and that specific surface features observed correlate uniquely with predicted chemical structures.
figures_summary: Figures show STM images comparing surfaces before and after annealing at various temperatures (175°C to 400°C), illustrating island formation and structural changes. DFT energy barrier diagrams map the minimum energy pathway for P-Si exchange, confirming stability of the P-Si-Br heterodimer.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for atomic precision doping; it details the combined STM/DFT approach; results show initial observations at low temperatures (175°C); DFT calculations confirm the stable product and calculate the minimum energy pathway, correlating theory with direct experimental observation of single-atom exchange.
why_interesting: While focused on materials science, the precise control over atomic incorporation pathways and the use of *in situ* characterization techniques are highly relevant to understanding quantum interfaces or defect engineering in solid-state quantum devices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Adsorption of PBr3 on Si(100)(a) at room temperature (b) followed by consecutive 5-minute anneals to 175◦C (c), 220◦C (d), and 400◦C (e). Empty-state STM images (7.5×7.5 nm2) were acquired at Us = +2 V, It = 2 nA, and a sample temperature of 77 K. Following dissociative adsorption of PBr3, P atoms are observed in the end-bridge (Peb) and bridge (Pbr) positions. Br atoms occupy on-top sites above Si atoms, predominantly in pairs on a single Si dimer. Annealing leads to the formation of silicon islands. Depressions, which are suggested to be embedded P atoms, are marked with squares (object A). Depressions adjacent to a protrusion, are marked by rectangles (object B). (f) Top-view...

FIG. 2. (a) The Si(100) surface after PBr3 adsorption. (b) The same area following annealing at 300◦C for 1 minute, revealing phosphorus incorporation. Frames (c, d) show atomic-resolution STM images before and after heating. In (a), structure Seb is indicated by a dotted line. In (b) and (d), a depressions adjacent to a protrusion is marked by a rectangle (object B), and a white arrows show the displacement of a Si bivacancy after heating. The white contour indicates water fragments OH and H before and after annealing. Empty-state STM images, 27×12 nm2 (a, b) and 6.2×6.2 nm2 (c, d), were acquired at Us = +2 V, It = 2 nA, and a temperature of 300 K.

FIG. 3. Identiﬁcation of the phosphorus incorporation sites. (a) Empty-state STM image (Us = +2.5 V, It = 3.0 nA, 300 K) of the Si(100) surface with adsorbed PBr3 after annealing to 300◦C for 1 minute. (b–e) Top-view models and simulated empty-state STM images with an embedded P atom and/or an adsorbed Br atom. Si atoms are marked in gray for the top layer (large circles) and the next layer (small circles), Br in red, and P in blue. The green lines in (a) and (b) separate the dimer rows.

FIG. 4. Energy barrier diagram for the P incorporation upon ad- sorption of the PBr3 molecule on Si(100) from end-bridge Peb and bridge Pbr positions. The most favorable positions for phosphorus adsorption (Seb and Sbr) and incorporation (Sin1, Sin2, and Sin3) are shown on top. Although Sin3 is the most energetically favorable con- ﬁguration, the reaction pathway leading to it was not calculated, as it was not observed experimentally. Energies are given in electron- volts. The red number denotes the activation barrier, values are given relative to Seb . Si atoms are marked in gray for the top layer (large circles) and the next layer (small circles), Br in red, and the P in blue.

FIG. 5. Phosphorus dimer on the Si(100) surface. (a) Empty-state STM image (Us = +3.2 V, It = 3.0 nA, 77 K) of one of the bright objects formed after PBr3 adsorption on Si(100) at room tempera- ture. (b) Simulated empty-state STM image and (c) top-view model of the most stable conﬁguration of P2 on Si(100). (d) Energy barrier diagram for the P association from two P atoms in bridge positions within the dimer row. The red number denotes the activation barrier. Si atoms are marked in gray, Br atoms in red, and the P atom in blue.
